title: Modules Intro
story: Your main function has grown to 200 lines — types, helpers, validation, I/O, all in one file. Finding anything is a nightmare. You need chapters for your code, just like chapters in a book. Modules let you group related code together and give it a name.
why: Modules are the fundamental unit of code organization — they group related types and functions, control visibility, and prevent name collisions as programs grow beyond a single file.
analogy: A module is like a chapter in a textbook — Chapter 3 is 'Math Functions,' Chapter 4 is 'String Functions.' Each chapter contains related content, has a clear title, and you reference content by chapter and section: 'see chapter 3, section 2' (math_utils.add).
try_it: Create a `stats` module with `min(a, b)` and `max(a, b)` functions. Create a `temperature` module with `celsius_to_fahrenheit(c)` and `fahrenheit_to_celsius(f)`. Use them both in main. What happens if you define `fn add(a, b)` in BOTH modules? Can they coexist? (Yes — modules prevent name collisions!)
tips: Access module items with `module_name.item_name` — the dot connects the namespace to the item
A module can contain functions AND types — it's a self-contained unit of related code
common_mistakes: Forgetting the module prefix when calling a function — `add(3, 4)` instead of `math_utils.add(3, 4)`
Putting code outside the module block but calling it inside — module definitions are top-level, not inside functions
Making module names too long — `utility_functions_for_mathematical_operations` is painful to type; keep it concise
